growth_story.headline: Tourism has taken Bahamian income per person to a new high in 2024, but after two decades of shocks it stands little above where it was in 2002.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990, income per person in the Bahamas has moved in four eras, each shaped by how tourism fared. It fell by 1.2 percent a year in 1990–1997, at the end of what the IMF called a decade of low growth. It then rose by 1.7 percent a year in 1998–2006, as private money flowed into tourism, shipping and construction. From 2007 to 2016 it fell by 1.0 percent a year: the global crisis hit in 2009, when income per person dropped 5.4 percent, and in the mid-2010s government belt-tightening, the end of building work and uncertainty over when the Baha Mar resort would open held back spending. Since 2017 it has grown 2.0 percent a year, but that average hides Hurricane Dorian in 2019, a 20.3 percent fall in 2020 when the pandemic stopped tourism, and rebounds of 17.4 percent in 2021 and 10.6 percent in 2022. By 2024 income per person was at its highest yet, though only a little above the level it first reached in 2002.

growth_story.tension: The IMF and World Bank describe a strong post-Covid recovery, and growth since 2017 averages 2.0 percent a year. But much of that is ground won back after the 2020 collapse. Income per person in 2024 was only a little above its 2007 level and about where it first stood in 2002, so from 2006 to 2024 it grew just 0.4 percent a year. A smaller gap: the IMF dates a recovery to the mid-1990s, yet the data put 1990–1997 at -1.2 percent a year, because the falls of the early 1990s were deep.
